name: Conchucos Quechua
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 3 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Stewart, Anne M. 1984. New approaches to coping with stress: A case study in Conchucos Quechua. Work Papers of the Summer Institute of Linguistics, University of North Dakota Session 28: 193-212. DOI 10.31356/silwp.vol28.06
catalog_locator: sec. 3, p.196; sec. 2.2, p.195 (weight definition); sec. 2.3, p.195; sec. 4.1, p.199; sec. 4.2, p.201; sec. 4.3, pp.202-203; sec. 5, pp.205-206; sec. 6 summary, p.207; sec. 7, pp.208-209; Notes n.5 (p.210). pp.196 and 203 verified, remainder on read in full.
catalog_quote: In ConQ, word-level main stress typically falls on the penultimate syllable, secondary stress on the initial syllable, and tertiary stresses on alternating syllables preceding the penult. [p.196] ... Syllables containing long vowels are considered to be heavy for the purposes of stress assignment ... aw, ay, uy and iy represent diphthongs, which behave like the long vowels [p.195] ... Disyllabic words in ConQ are main-stressed initially (ie. penultimately) regardless of whether or not either or both syllables have branching nuclei. Vowel length in either syllable does attract secondary stress, however [p.199] ... Since final long vowels usually attract main stress when following a short penult, the metrical rules accomodate themselves economically to the realities of the language. [p.201] ... if a heavy final syllable is preceded by a light penult, the penult may still receive main stress. Stress always falls on the penultimate syllable in words ending in two heavy syllables [p.203] ... Heavy penults always attract main-stress. Heavy penults in three-syllable words include syllables with branching rimes (closed syllables) as well as branching nuclei ... Light penults preceded by a heavy initial never bear main stress ... Final heavy syllables may, but need not necessarily, bear main stress if and only if the preceding syllables are both light [p.205]
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: sout2992 is not in the catalog. Of the three title hits: Stewart 1984 (open, held by the project, read) is a first-hand metrical description: main stress penultimate, secondary initial, quantity-sensitive with optional final-heavy attraction and initial-stress variants in light trisyllables. Hintz 2006 (IJAL 72:477-521, DOI 10.1086/513058) is the best source but closed access (Unpaywall closed; JSTOR/UChicago/Academia/BASE/Benjamins all bot-challenged; Internet Archive offline; eScholarship WAF); its content is known only via Buchholz 2023 pp. 34-35 and Buchholz & Reich 2018 p. 131, which report an instrumental 4-speaker finding of INITIAL primary stress with penult secondary in connected speech, reversed under isolation/emphasis, no weight-sensitivity - i.e. it conflicts with Stewart. Izre'el 2020 is a Glottolog false hit (computerized language code from the word 'interfaces'; a Hebrew-based theoretical chapter on the utterance). Also held by the project and read: Buchholz 2023 sec. 7.1.1 (pp. 504-505) concludes Huari Quechua cares very little about word stress, with the penult a variable tonal anchoring site and no evidence for initial prominence. Priority acquisition: Hintz 2006 (high).

new_statements.rule_in_words: Default: primary stress on the penult, secondary on the word-initial syllable, rhythmic tertiary stresses leftward from the penult. Quantity (long vowels/diphthongs; in trisyllables also closed syllables) interferes: in words of four or more syllables a word-final long vowel after a light penult usually (but optionally) takes the main stress; if both final syllables are heavy the penult wins; disyllables are always penult(=initial)-stressed; in trisyllables a heavy penult is stressed, otherwise a heavy initial, otherwise optionally a heavy final, and all-light trisyllables vary between initial and penult. Stress is stated to be rarely contrastive at word level.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Secondary stress on the word-initial syllable; tertiary on alternating syllables preceding the penult; long vowels consistently attract (at least) secondary stress (pp.196, 199, 203).
new_statements.exceptions: Optional final main stress on word-final long vowels (e.g. 1st-person length) after a light penult; -shkaa '1st person perfect' always main-stressed (lexically marked, p.206); initial-stress variants of all-light trisyllables (yakuman ~ yakuman, p.198); -kuna, kaq and often -pis open a new stress domain, and clitics -pita, -lla(-raq), -ta, -na, -qa may be extrametrical giving antepenultimate stress (pp.208-209); two content words may form one stress domain (p.208).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level ('lexical') stress from texts, isolated words and phrases (field data 1979-82); author notes the stress domain is not always the grammatical word (sec. 7). NB modern instrumental work disagrees: Hintz 2006 (as reported by Buchholz 2023: 34) finds initial primary stress in connected speech and penult primary stress in isolation/emphasis; Buchholz 2023: 504-505 finds Huari Quechua 'cares very little about word stress', with the word penult only a variable anchoring site for phrase-level tones and no initial prominence.
new_statements.identity_note: Stewart 1984 labels the variety 'Conchucos Quechua' (eastern Ancash, area bounded by Pomabamba in the north and San Marcos in the south); Glottolog files it under sout2992, but Buchholz 2023: 34 fn.24 notes that Stewart's 1987 data came largely from a community near Pomabamba, i.e. the northern edge (Northern Conchucos Ancash Quechua, nort2980), so the 1984 stress data may straddle qxn/qxo. Hintz 2006 (not opened) is on speakers from Huaripampa near San Marcos (South Conchucos proper); Buchholz 2023 and Buchholz & Reich 2018 are on 'Huari Quechua' = South Conchucos Quechua of Huari town/province (sout2992).

sources.note: First-hand AM/OT analysis of Huari (South Conchucos) Quechua prosody from semi-spontaneous dialogue data: no lexical tone; pitch contours are assigned at the phonological-phrase / accentual-phrase level (compared to Japanese, French, Korean), with a post-lexical inventory of three PhP/AP tonal patterns — rising LH, falling HL, rising-falling LHL — whose choice signals continuation vs finality and only marginally utterance type; phrase-final tonal movements align like boundary tones rather than pitch accents on a stressed syllable; phrase-final devoicing can leave the 'stressed' penult low or…

tone.quote: the analysis in this study has found Huari Quechua to be an example of a language that can be said to “care” very little about word stress in the sense of Hyman (2014). That is to say, there is evidence for stress, but it is quite subtle. ... Pitch contours have been found to be assigned at the level of the phonological phrase (PhP) / accentual phrase (AP), as e.g. in Japanese, French, or Korean ... Phrase-final tonal movements show temporal alignment behaviour that is more indicative of boundary tones than of pitch accents associated with word stress ... The Huari Quechua tonal inventory ... consists of three observed PhP/AP-level tonal patterns: a rising (LH), a falling (HL), and a rising-falling (LHL) pattern.

sources.quote: Buchholz 2023: 34 (summarizing Hintz 2006): "Unlike the previous studies, Hintz (2006) uses instrumental acoustic data in her study on stress in South Conchucos Quechua. She does not find evidence for weight-sensitivity ... Based on data from four speakers, she finds that stress is word-initial in spontaneous connected speech, with a secondary stress on the penult. In isolated words and under conditions of "emphasis", the situation reverses, and primary stress is now located on the penult, with secondary stress on the initial syllable."
